en: The instruction for Lakṣmī’s Consort is the protection of the Vedic syllables; this four-verse hymn bestows prosperity upon the wicked-minded Rākṣasas, just as it did for Lakṣmī’s Consort.
Before a consonant (*hal*), a consonant (*hal*) is doubled; likewise, a contact consonant (*sparśa*) following *l* or *v* is doubled after a vowel that has a following *ū* or *rdhva*.

When followed by a consonant (*hal*), the first two [consonants] may optionally be doubled before a consonant (*vāci vā hal*). Furthermore, when preceded by a short vowel (*hrasvāt*), the final *n* and *ṅ* (*anta-ganaṅau*) are doubled, provided they are accompanied by a nasal (*anusvāra*) at the beginning [of the doubled group], and this doubling occurs mutually between them. This applies also to those following *ava* and *para*.
Two hundred and two [letters] are also from the preceding *āgama*; here, the two consonants (*ha* and *la*) follow the fourth and the second [vowels].
In the case of *bhūte*, the word *dhāma* follows; this is the supreme [path] beyond the end.
What are those that go before? They are the upward-moving prefixes; sometimes they go before according to the mark of the three-armed one (*cikhibhuja*).

In that [group], the first consonant among the unvoiced sibilants (*aghoṣoṣman*)—even when there is a similar contact (*sadṛśasparśa*)—should take the first vowel from above or below; it does not take the last (*anta*), nor the second, nor the sibilant (*uṣman*), provided it is followed by a consonant other than the final one (*anuttama*). However, [this rule applies] starting from the first vowel, not from the last.

In the case of the best [vowels], there is no *visarga* before the best [consonants]; nor is there *lopa* of a *ha* followed by a *sparśa*. Nor is there *lopa* of a *na* when followed by a *sparśa*. A *ma* preceded by *ya*, *va*, or *ha* does not become doubled; rather, it takes its nasal counterpart (*anunāsika*) from among the *y*, *v*, *l*, *s*, or a *sparśa* that is homogeneous (*savarṇa*) with it. 3.
After a nasal, the augment *ka* and the substitution of *ga* shall occur respectively for the following *dh* and *bh*.
After a nasal, *ka* is substituted for *kha*, and after a nasal other than *ṅ*, *ta* is substituted for *tha*.

Following a stop that is not a sibilant (*ūṣman*), when followed by stops situated above [the row] or by the highest [nasals], they are called *yamas*; likewise, those that are not highest [are also called *yamas*].
In the Yajurveda, the nasal sound *ṇa* is joined with *na* and *ma*; for an *aṅga* preceded by *acch*, *ka* is substituted.

Having mastered the four verses on the sequence of phonemes (*varṇakrama*) both in recitation and in meaning—O you who are experts in the sequence of phonemes—may you be victorious in the ten directions!
Thus ends the instruction of Lakṣmīkānta;
having bowed at the lotus feet of Nārāyaṇa, [this] instruction of Lakṣmīkānta [is concluded].
I shall perform the determination of the high pitch (ucca-svara) by reciting and analyzing the words of the Vedas, which removes the suffering of all the three worlds.

No rule has been established by anyone regarding any accentual characteristic such as this: that a word is oxytone, or that this initial syllable is high-pitched, or that it is of such a kind; nor is there a rule for the single-substitute (ekādeśa) resulting from the *yav* replacement when it occurs in *saṃhitā*.
That which is the object of the definition, even if it is unaccented, is [the subject];
this treatise is composed in order to know that a word is of two kinds—namely, that which has the accent on the final syllable and likewise that which has the accent on the initial syllable. (3–4)
In this context, first the low-pitched vowel is taken according to the sequence beginning with 'a',
and then the high-pitched vowel is taken according to the sequence of the eyes (two);
here, the diversity of words that have become gestural (iṅgita) is intended.

The words that are separated, followed by others, and have their final syllables accented on the last vowel— such as *adya*, *anyaḥ*, *aśvataraḥ*, *asya*, *arkaḥ*, *aśnuvīta*, *aṅgān*, *aśvaḥ*, *apratim*, *abhiprītāḥ*,
*ukhā-pūrvaḥ*, *asya*, *uśāna*, *edīśvaraḥ*, and *paraḥ*— are [to be treated as such].
Asāmā, Antaḥrājā, Ācārya, Mākavākṣṇayāvama,
Anyādhicaraṇa, Ardhya, Asthān, Aṣṭame, Aṣṭāṣṭakā, likewise Āmayāvin, Āṅgirasa, Etau, Āptvāptātma, and Ārtava.
The Ārta, the Rālikhita, the Āgneyī, the Ārambha, the Āśvinī, the Ādityā, the Āgrayaṇī, and the Tṛṣṇeṣṭi— these are the portions of the *agraha* (the first portion).
"May they be for me here, impelled by desire, kindled here"— thus [speaks] the Lord, the Sovereign.
With the *īrmāntāsaḥ*, the *arvākṣasaḥ*, the *ukṣaṇaḥ*, the *ūtī*, the *ūrjā*, and likewise with the *ūrdhvārciḥ* and the *ṛcā*;
and with this eleventh [verse], these [cups] belong to Indra. One should perform the Aindravāyava cup with these; how was it previously given? How was it performed?
Having done so, the dark and emaciated chest, the doer, and likewise the cruel one;
by means of a jar, Kāvya, having gone with hunger and seized [it] with the voice of a donkey; Gāyatrī and the singer of Gāyatrī, as well as the terrible one and the one smeared with ghee.

Candracandrā is in the fourth; Canacitra is also in the fourth. Having piled it in the intermediate space, one should pile it; he piles it as previously directed. Chāyā and having covered, she remained; "Slay the enemy! [he says].
Having conquered, the progenitor tongue, rejoicing, has been fashioned for thee from the born body;
it is honeyed, having attained life, O Amba, may Bṛhaspati protect thee; sharp, satisfied, and swift-moving, as if with curd, he has looked toward the quarters.
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is to be given at the tenth [stage] on each successive day of initiation;
having initiated [the sacrificer], the divine quarters and the goddesses of the quarters [are to be honored];
may there be the movement of the gods and the restraint of obstacles in the intermediate directions and in the heavens.

The supporter, the upholder, the steadfast one, the ordainer; through wisdom he is established in the ninth. Is it not indeed Nārāśaṃsa? Then there is the leader by boat, Pūṣan, who on the path was the nourisher of old; the son of the earth, the father of the earth.
Parameṣṭhin, Priya, Parṇa, Paryārin, Parama, Pṛṇa, Prasthātṛ, Prathama, Paṅkti, Pāvaka, Parama, Padāpatya,
Preṇa, Piśāṅga, Pavayitṛ, and Piśāṅgila.
The words *prokṣitāḥ*, *iṣitāḥ*, *iddhaḥ*, *āpnumukṣitaḥ*, *akṣitam*,
and *utetiraśitam* occur as the fifth [word] in these subsequent [verses].
Then Piṅgalā was questioned by her father; likewise Bṛhatī, Bārhaspatyā, Brahmā, and Brāhmaṇa;
and having become bound, having struck, having devoured, and having pierced—[he asked].
The portion has become manifest; having become such an appearance through abundance,

it is wise, free from conflict, great through its greatness, delightful, inspired thought, soft from within, a destroyer of affliction, for the mother, Mitra, the son of Mitrā-Varuṇa, and the descendant of Manu.
Having cleansed [the altar], likewise the Mother, Māyā, and the Head;
and Guñcā, Mādhā—do you two perform the sacrifice at the rite, being well-disposed; come hither for splendor!
May she be pleasant and ever gracious in the dwelling, and then worthy of sacrifice.
Gold and the upper garment— these two are not prescribed for the ancestors;
[there is] the month-long [vow], the extended begging, sacrifice within sacrifice, when Yama [is present], with broth, he who has yoked this [chariot], the sacrificer, and she who is at the yoking.
Roke, Rajatā, Rātri, Rudrā, Rayi, Atha, Rudra, Rūpī,
Rudra, Rākā, Rūpā, Raktvā— thus she is called in the world; Leśe, Vaśā, Vasnāvidāna, and Viśvavāstu.
By the water indeed, by the path indeed, having turned yourself;
by the free people, by the Varuṇa-law, you are entered, entered as the speaker;
upon the reed, the year, the wielder of the thunderbolt; let the twentyfold speech be divided.
Thus ends the Lakṣmīkāntaśikṣā.
